newsitem.title: USA: California budget plan to reform welfare, cut taxes.
newsitem.headline: California budget plan to reform welfare, cut taxes.

text.p: California Gov. Pete Wilson Thursday proposed a $67 billion state spending plan that would dramatically change the state welfare system, cut taxes and boost education spending.
"This is more than a spending plan," Wilson told reporters at a Sacramento briefing on his budget proposal for the 1997-1998 fiscal year starting July 1.

The Republican governor said his far-reaching budget would "end welfare" and pump billions of dollars into schools to "guarantee a future of peace, prosperity and opportunity for our children, and our children's children."

Democrats, who control both houses of the state legislature which must approve the budget, said they would work from Wilson's blueprint. But some voiced concerns that his welfare reform plan was too harsh and that his proposed business tax cut would be too costly.

Citing rosy forecasts for economic growth, Wilson said state spending would be kept below revenues. He said that in 1997 California was expected to become the first state in the nation with an economic output of over $1 trillion.
In line with federal law, the governor's welfare proposal would set a state lifetime limit of five years on aid, including time on aid in other states.
But under Wilson's plan, starting from 1998, able-bodied people currently on welfare may only receive aid for a total of 24 months during any 36-month period.
New recipients may only receive aid for 12 months during any 24-month period. Wilson said some exemptions would be provided for those unable to care for themselves.
In addition, Wilson said grants would be reduced by 15 percent for most recipients after six months on assistance.
Wilson's welfare plan drew fire from some Democrats concerned that it was too harsh.
"It appears the governor's proposal tends more towards punishing poor people rather than assisting people," state Senate President Bill Lockyer, a Democrat, said.
Wilson's proposal to cut the state's bank and corporation tax by 10 percent over two years also came under attack.

Assembly Speaker Cruz Bustamante, a Democrat, said he would prefer more targeted tax relief and state Senator Mike Thompson, chairman of the Senate Budget Committee, said the tax cuts would be a drain on the state budget.
Republicans and Democrats generally praised Wilson's school funding program which would keep primary and secondary education the state's top spending priority at $21 billion.
